title: Dublin Glasco watchmakers
standfirst: The 1773 advertisement names Philip as the father of Thomas the watchmaker. The preferred working model identifies the son with Margaret Duffy’s husband, Thomas Glasco-144, and the father with the elder Philip Glasco-146: probable,67%. The competing Thomas identities remain open.
question: Can a primary record connect the Dublin watchmakers and distinguish the competing Thomas profiles?
answer: The selected uncertain model places the provisional elder account Glasco-146 under Thomas Glasgow-1242 through possible identity with the 1711 Scottish child Glasgow-1241. No migration is proved. The two younger accounts, Glasco-147 and Glasgow-3932, retain their existing strong same-person match; the latter’s misplaced Kilrea biography now has a complete sourced Dublin replacement queued locally. No live merge or save has been made. Philip Glasco senior and junior are separately reported as watchmakers. The 1779 Christchurch Lane marriage notice and the 1783 Ormond Quay directory very probably concern one Thomas watchmaker. The maintained 1773 advertisement reading explicitly names his father Philip. Identifying the tradesman with the 1773 Margaret Duffy groom, and the named Philip with the elder account Glasco-146, is now the selected probable father proposition at67%. It replaces the unsupported Thomas-173 attachment locally, with the former father retained as an uncertain alternative. No live save, merge or new mother follows.

chapters.title: Dublin: Philip is the preferred father of Thomas, 67%
body: Research rationale: use the combined Dublin family and trade evidence to select a useful working parent, with its unresolved identities explicit.

Select Philip Glasco-146, the provisional elder Dublin watchmaker account, as the probable working father of Thomas Glasco-144 at 67% subjective confidence. The maintained reading of the 1773 advertisement explicitly says that Thomas served his apprenticeship to his father Philip Glasco and subsequently practised in London before returning to his father’s Christ-Church-lane house. Thomas’s 12 December 1773 marriage to Margaret Duffy at neighbouring St Audoen’s supplies a particular same-name adult, same year and immediate locality, rather than a Scotland-wide name comparison. A young tradesman returning to the family business and marrying later that year is the preferred explanation. The later Christ-Church-lane to 20 Ormond Quay sequence supports continuity of the watchmaking business. The separate marriage and apprenticeship evidence together justify preferring Philip to the unsupported Thomas-173 father attachment.

The 67% rates the complete profile-level father proposition, including identification of the 1773 groom with the advertised watchmaker and of the named Philip with the elder account. Neither the marriage index nor the Duffy pedigree gives Thomas’s trade, address or father’s forename. The advertisement is reused from the 7 October full-page OCR reading; its original image was not newly inspected. The older Philip account contains some junior events, so the elder/junior distinction remains material. Thomas’s circa 1753 birth is an estimate: age twenty would make completed apprenticeship plus several years in London compressed, favouring a somewhat older adult without establishing a replacement birth year. No date is changed. The rare surname, close locality and year are correlated clues, not independent parent statements.

Retain Thomas Glasco-173 as an unselected, previously ungraded father alternative, and retain a distinct unrepresented Thomas watchmaker as an identity alternative. Thomas-173, father with Catherine of Sarah in 1760, is chronologically compatible with the trade cluster, but connecting that household to the 1773 groom adds an unsupported generation, whereas the advertisement names Philip. Thomas-143 could represent the tradesman only if his very weak circa 1766 estimate is revised; the date is not a hard exclusion. The 1779 Miss Hynes marriage and the 1785 Mary King licence may concern remarriages, but no spouse death or identity bridge establishes that sequence. No merge, new wife or new child follows.

The current Catherine Mangan mother attachment and Thomas-143 child attachment remain separately ungraded; Philip’s spouse is not thereby proved to be Thomas’s mother. The selected father replaces one existing local working attachment. Two already-catalogued descendants move into the main working component; the old Thomas-173 account remains separate. No new person, live WikiTree edit or confidence-only upgrade is claimed. The earlier Scottish ancestry assigned to Philip remains uncertain and does not become probable through this change.

Check the original 1773 advertisement and marriage entry, the Duffy 1774/1775 probate papers, and Thomas’s London apprenticeship/freedom records for trade, address or named kin. Seek the 1777 Margaret Glasco grant and the full 1777 Philip/Thomas chancery bill before accepting a Duffy–Hynes remarriage or a precise Philip generation.

chapters.period: 1711–1772 · uncertain Scottish ancestry and biography correction
chapters.title: Selected elder father and younger Philip biography correction
body: Select Thomas Glasgow-1242 as the uncertain working father of Philip Glasco-146. The preferred model uses Glasco-146 as the elder Dublin watchmaker account, retaining the 1711 Scottish child Glasgow-1241 as a separate possible account of the same man. That child’s Uphall index names father Thomas; his existing research already retains the elder watchmaker as a compatible adult identity. The Glasco-146 account has the Christ Church Lane watchmaking association in 1752, an estimated birth about 1715 and a younger Philip in its tree family, which suit that provisional elder role. The four-year difference from the 1711 baptism is between a record and an unsupported estimate, not a concrete identity conflict. This materialises the existing Scottish candidate at low confidence; it does not prove migration or two distinct elder Philips.

The Dublin records name no Scottish parents, birthplace or apprenticeship, so the Scottish child and elder watchmaker may be different men. The fresh Glasco-146 biography itself mixes the 1752 watchmaker with junior notices of 1765,1768 and 1770. Its c.1715 birth and the c.1740 birth of Glasco-147 are tree estimates, not evidence selecting a generation. If Glasco-146 instead represents the junior, the elder Philip is an alternative father-generation placement and the Thomas link would need revision; no competing father is attached alongside it. The elder placement is a preferred working interpretation of the profile’s trade/address and family structure, not a claim that every event in that biography belongs to him. The junior’s 1765 unnamed-wife death,1768 Teresa Plunkett marriage and reported 1770 death remain with the younger documentary account Glasgow-3932. Glasco-147 is a strongly supported duplicate account of that younger man, but its quoted 1772 younger/inventory wording was not independently rechecked here and establishes neither the estimated birth nor a newly verified father clause; a grant date is not a death date. No merge, spouse transfer or new child attachment follows. Catherine Mangan is called Glasco-146’s mother in its prose but spouse in its structured family; the 1750 report describes the elder’s bride only as the widow Mangan, and the 1760 report gives no forename. Neither record proves maternity. Preserve the existing Mangan/Braccan and younger-parent fields as qualified leads; do not add a mother for Glasco-146. The father Thomas is common to the retained 1711 child records, while the 3 June Uphall versus 21 October Linlithgow Philip entries and their maternal readings remain unreconciled; Jean Duncan is not transferred as Glasco-146’s mother. The 1777 probate/court occurrence does not establish survival after 1772. The local elder account uses 1772 as an uncertain death year through the selected identity, retaining the old after 1772 value and all junior events in the comparison.

The anonymous Open-profile capture of Glasgow-3932 on 16 October 2026 contains Robert Glasgow’s Kilrea 1827 biography, not the Dublin watchmaker. The entire misplaced text is also preserved in the captured biography of the correct Robert Glasgow-3897. A complete sourced Dublin replacement is prepared locally; the real current biography remains available in the comparison, with its hash retained. No Robert birth, relatives or life events are transferred to Philip. The structured Dublin profile and the current Glasco-147/Teresa Plunkett family support retaining the earlier strong same-person match between the two younger-Philip profiles, without a live merge or duplicate spouse attachment.

chapters.title: Two named Philips
body: A 1750 marriage notice calls Philip Glasco senior an eminent watchmaker of Christchurch Lane; a 1760 notice reports his wife's death.
A younger Philip, also a Christchurch watchmaker, married Teresa Plunkett in 1768 and died in Christ Church Lane in 1770. The notices do not state the two men were father and son.

chapters.title: One likely travelling address
body: A 1779 notice places Thomas Glasco, watchmaker, at Christchurch Lane when he married Miss Hynes of Ormond Quay. Watson's 1783 directory lists Thomas Glasco, watchmaker, at 20 Ormond Quay.
The uncommon name, occupation and apparent move to the bride's street strongly support one tradesman. They do not identify him with any existing Thomas profile.
